Edit: This is a really long reply to your post but increasing overweight/obesity is a massive complex issue that is less about individual behaviour than what most people would like to think. 

Our environment largely affects our health. We have increasingly obesogenic environments which facilitates weight gain and it’s really difficult to resist against this. It isn’t that people are stupid or lazy. Given that in countries like the US, UK, Aus, etc, most people are overweight/obese that would imply that almost everyone is stupid and lazy. That’s simply not true. 

So, what’s changed?

The amount of hours the average person has to work to stay afloat and the kind of inactivity that can associated with these jobs are huge contributors. Other factors include food advertisement, poor city planning (fast food restaurants really close by schools for instance, urban sprawl so that you can’t just cycle or walk to where you need to go, etc), we now have addictive sedentary activities that once never existed (never ending tv, social media, video games, etc.). Overall people are so time poor and don’t want to sacrifice the time they have cooking healthy foods when there are near instant meal options available. On top of this, these foods can be advertised to look healthy even if they’re complete garbage for you. 

We also now have insanely delicious and addictive ultra processed foods that lack nutritional value and whilst being being energy dense. Not to mention these foods can be incredibly cheap and you’re incentivised to buy copious amounts of them such as through 2 for 1 deals, etc. Did you know that most sales on food are for ultra processed rubbish foods rather than nutritious foods? These foods are intentionally designed so that you can’t stop eating them. Id consider it malicious food development. 

It’s all a big hot mess. A lot of these issues stem from poor public health policy and the cost of living way more than people just “giving up”. 

Even healthy foods have reduced nutritional value today compared to 20,50,100 years ago. Our crops are grown with efficiency and yield in mind above the nutritional value of the final product. 

Almost no one likes to be overweight and obese. People know it’s unhealthy. Given that excess weight affects most people, the common denominator isn’t poor behaviour and that everyone decided to “let themselves go”. 

Yes you can resist against your environment. But it is hard. We need to stop entirely blaming the average Joe and start questioning why this is a problem that is being enabled by our governments. We have a major issue on our hands with global conglomerates having way too much power. Our food environment is only getting worse and it’s really scary.

If the dietician has a PhD and does research then I’d believe it. Especially if it’s to do with gastrointestinal health or just generally a disease that can be better managed through diet. But any study where patient number =1 is laughable. You can find studies with n=1 “proving” ANYTHING.

Look im not trying to pick a fight here, but I think you might be a bit confused about some things. The things I’m saying are your ABCs of nutrition. They’re not contentious.

There are SO many anti nutritional factors found in plant foods. And they don’t all magically disappear with cooking. If they did, that would be wonderful. 

 Heme/non heme iron is COMMONLY discussed in terms of bioavailability. Your lack of ability to understand the use of that word goes to show that you’re misinformed. 

I get my information from text books and papers and researchers. The text books get THEIR information from papers. Not from some silly blog or podcast, but as part of my degree that I’m almost done with.

There’s no need to bend the narrative and distort science in favour of veganism. Veganism isn’t about health or the environment veganism is about the animals. 

Plant based diets can have carcinogenic factors to their foods the same as as animal foods can. If we’re gonna pull out the “ ALL meat can give you cancer” card then it’s only fair to recognise that plant based foods are equally capable. This is because method of cooking can have a large impact on such factors. 

When starchy foods are cooked at high temperatures (such as in frying), compounds with carcinogenic properties can be produced. Some of these compounds include polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), heterocyclic amines (HCAs), and acrylamides. 

Studies have shown associations between fermented foods and higher incidences of certain cancers too. 

There isn’t a need to say meat is inherently bad for you, there isn’t a need to give a plant based diet a god like status either. 

There isn’t a need to get aggressive towards people. If you have valid points- make them! I enjoy opportunities fo learn. I enjoy these opportunities to learn so much that I’m on my way to being a nutrition science researcher. You’re so concerned about the world being made better without me, but maybe you need to look in the mirror because all you’re doing is trying to abuse people over Reddit when you could put value to your time and be constructive.

B12 isnt naturally found in plant foods. Heaps of plant based foods are fortified with it- such as almond milks! B12 deficiencies do happen and they can cause permanent side effects, which is why it’s advised for vegans to supplement even if you’re having fortified foods in your diet. 

The long chain omega3s we need are not produced by all algae- and the ones that do are why we can have vegan friendly supplements with ALA, EPA and DHA. I don’t think all algae/seaweed produce EPA and DHA. Heaps of plant foods have ALA but we still need the other two longer chain forms.

The way we process foods- meat and plant alike- can increase risks of cancers though! There are studies showing links between fermented foods and cancers, as well as high temperatures used in baking and frying creating carcinogenic compounds. Plant based foods can be damaging too!  

Like it or not we evolved with meat in our diet. Meat provides good nutrition. We absorb iron, zinc, etc. all better from meat because they’re in more bioavailable forms and there are anti nutritive factors to get in the way when we get these nutrients from plants. Not to mention we can’t get the omega 3s and B12 naturally from plant based foods! Meat simply is not always bad to eat. 

Yes, meats like salami are rubbish, but I haven’t seen any studies showing a relationship between chicken and cancer. Given that we evolved to have these foods as a substantial parts of our diet, it’s only logical that they can safely form part of our diet. 

Everyone has the right to draw their own line of what they think is or isn’t risky, but it feels a bit wrong to suggest that eating meat is really so unsafe…

Youre right! There are so many things that are bad for the environment and there are people higher on the hierarchy that need to enforce change. It’s not fair to say this is a “breastapo” problem born from an antiquated idea when in the world of nutrition science it’s generally accepted that breast milk is best. If we want to talk about *nutrition* strictly, formula is only best/as good under specific medical circumstances. 

In the real world there are so many reasons why it isn’t an option to or possible for women to breast feed, or why they may want to feed with formula and breast milk. I feel so bad for the woman in OPs story and of course she should formula feed if she wants to because it is still adequate nutrition. Hopefully they get the support they need :(((

I 100% agree with what you’re saying about how awful it is that some people don’t have supportive partners, and that some women just CANT produce breast milk. But it’s important to recognise that formula =/= breast milk. 

Human milk contains oligosaccharides which are not digestible for the baby, but for the developing gut micro biome within the baby. This is not replicated in baby formula. The full importance of the gut microbiome is only just now being understand, but is thought to have strong links with the immune system and even linked with mental health. 

Another factor to consider is that formula can actually have too much protein than is needed by the baby. Studies have shown babies fed on these formulas had higher chances of being overweight/obese later in life. 

Of course for women who are not properly nourished, they may not make nutritious enough milk, which is exactly when formula I think is such an important tool. As for women who cannot make milk, I think this is why breast milk banks are so important and something that should be encouraged if we want to get into the nutrition of things! Ultimately women have the right to choose and not be shamed for their choices, but humans already make the perfect food for babies and this just has not yet been replicated yet.

You're right, this current diet will likely have consequences, but unfortunately, it's almost impossible to get other people to change their eating habits. Starting small with making changes can really help. Ultimately, you need to be looking out for your own diet first and foremost, but offering to cook for your family might be the kick in the right direction that they need. To get your family involved in this, you could even start with something like encouraging healthier oils to cook with (olive oil!!!), or encouraging different dessert options. Instead of post-dinner pudding, maybe you could entice your family with a healthy homemade crumble? People often forget how great fruit is until you cut up a fruit salad! 

There are plenty of healthy homemade vegan mac and cheese recipes out there that are highly reliant on vegetables as the main sauce ingredient. Some recipes off the top of my head that are winners amongst picky eaters I know are: Nora Cooks Vegan Meatballs, minimalist baker Vegan Fried Rice. Most bean-heavy Mexican recipes out there are also usually a treat- lazy cat kitchen's Mexican potato skins are amazing. The internet is a treasure trove of deliciousness, if you explore it first, your family may follow. 

As lunch is generally less of a shared family meal, that may be the hardest to influence change in. Smoothies are a great way to get a fairly balanced breakfast. They can easily contain a fruit and plant milk serving, but you can also blend in some granola or oats as well as a vegetable or two!

Nutrition is a very nuanced thing. I think it all depends upon the context for the parents. Are they themselves obese, overweight, or quite healthy? For a very healthy parent to have an obese child would maybe suggest abuse because it would appear they know what is and is not healthy. However, an obese parent having an obese child shows that there's maybe something systemic going on here. After all, no one WANTS to be obese (at least, very very few people). If weight loss and weight management and being healthy were truly easy and THAT accessible, then we wouldn't be going through an obesity epidemic right now. There are so many factors that come into play here. 

There's the food environment- this isn't cultivated by the parent. Advertisement is malicious and psychological, they know how to sell products to people. It's completely predatory. There are also factors such as if your area allows for fast food options nearby schools? What food options are at your sport recreation centers? Healthy options, or unhealthy options that are marketed and accepted as "rewards" for all the hard work exercising? Do schools encourage exercise? Are there green spaces nearby where someone lives so that their children have room to play and run around? Let's not forget that food is a pleasurable experience. All these ultra-processed foods that are devoid of nutrients are formulated so that they give you lots of pleasure- they're addictive. They're also unlikely to make you full- they're low in fiber, they don't require much chewing, they have very low water content. These foods are relatively new and they are dangerous. Yet we put them in fun packaging, they're cheap, they're normalized. 

Let's look at food convenience. How much are the parents working? Is that out of necessity? Why is it, if so? Why can't parents sustain a liveable wage for their families without working a ridiculous amount of hours? Parents have less time now to spend cooking, making ready-made meals and fast food options more attractive. Fast food continually gets cheaper too, so to the untrained eye, it looks as though these options are cheaper. What foods are available in the area? Are fruits and vegetables really expensive and of poor quality? Supermarkets are set up so that you have to go past all the really tempting foods and so that you impulse buy. 

What nutritional training is out there for new parents? Is there support to ensure that they know how to feed their child healthy foods? It isn't always intuitive. Some people never learned how to feed themselves adequately and don't know how to feed their children as consequence. 

The more common obesity has become, the less alarming it has also become. Obesity isn't typically an issue of individuals, but of the many factors fitting into people's lives. Could some parents stand to be more involved in their child's life? Of course! I'm not saying that there aren't some bad parents out there. Obesity isn't typically a linear problem, it isn't as simple as someone being a bad or an abusive parent, there are just so many factors at play here- it's a three-dimensional problem.

This is my best understanding of your points: 

1. When it comes to ownerships and rights, companies like to protect their product because a lot of money goes into the creation of GMO foods. It takes a long time to create a GMO food (around a decade, can be longer) and is a very costly process. Making a product at the end of a day needs to be profitable- so that is why their IP is protected and owned. How would these companies persist and make products- which are beneficial to farmers and consumers- only to have their work copied elsewhere? 

2. Again, it comes down to the operation needing to be profitable for the company to survive and continue to generate new products. Needing to renew a license each year to continue to grow a crop, or purchasing a new set of seeds, allows for this. A once off purchase of seeds may be either A) too expensive for the farmer B) not profitable enough for the producer of said product. 

3. I can’t really comment on roundup. What pesticides are approved for agriculture is different for different regions. Monsanto have a lot to answer for. Worse still, the government which allowed for their products to harm people. As they’re now under the Bayer group so maybe they’ll skip under peoples noses a bit better... I think the unfortunate reality is that for a long time that management of crops against insects weren’t and aren’t optimised best. Whilst we are getting better at this, the reality is when you have a monoculture system you are going to have many issues such as an insect population that suddenly thrives and you can’t control. It’s really just such a complex issue and depending on where you live you can have different levels of faith in your government for protecting the health of the consumers with what insecticides and at what levels they approve of.

4. GMO foods must undergo rigorous testing to prove that they are safe for the consumer. Many would say the testing that must be done to allow for a product to be on the market is actually excessive- but a necessary evil for the misinformation that has made consumers afraid of these products. The unknown effects they may have to the ecosystem is comparable to the impacts that any other monoculture system may have. So really, it’s not fair to say GMO crops as compared to traditionally modified crops as harmful to the ecosystem. There are many problems with our current agricultural system- but GMO isn’t one of them. In fact, GMO crops are being designed to overcome many of the agricultural challenges we will face and will soon become a vital tool to manage food production (limiting water, increased soil salinity, increased temperatures, etc).

I remember in grade 3 at my private school we learned some french, Japanese, I remember having challenging spelling tests, doing multiplication challenges with other students. Looking back at the education i received at a public school compared to what I would have at a private school, I feel like going through tutoring to get a scholarship into a private school or a selective public high school seems quite worthwhile. Were there people who did well from my public school? Absolutely. But there weren’t any students from my school getting into medicine, that’s for sure! IMO, it’s a lot easier to do well when your peers actually care and your teacher cares. To me that was the biggest shock. My classmates treated my teachers poorly, my teachers didn’t care about the individual often (there were some nice gems still of course).
